question: If classic case-based classifiers (kNN, decision trees, and a labeled k-means variant called L-means) are fitted on a neural language model's penultimate-layer representations and used for prediction instead of the neural head, do they preserve predictive performance while making every decision faithfully attributable to specific training examples, and does that attribution support removal-based contestation of decisions better than influence-function baselines?

key_findings.claim: Wrapper boxes replace the neural classification head with classic case-based models on extracted penultimate representations, and the faithfulness claim is scoped to the wrapper classifier, which does not approximate the neural model and can disagree with it.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4 states that the pipeline mean-pools penultimate-layer token states into sentence vectors, fits kNN/DT/L-means on them, and that 'wrapper boxes do not attempt to approximate the underlying neural model, i.e., wrapper box vs. neural model predictions can differ'; the derived example-based explanations 'faithfully explain the inference procedure of the wrapper boxes, not the original neural model'.

anchors.section: 4 Wrapper Boxes and 4.1 Learning Feature Representations

key_findings.claim: Predictive performance of the wrapper boxes is largely comparable to the fine-tuned transformers: only 6/48 comparisons differ significantly on TOXIGEN (3 favoring the wrapper) and 13/48 on E-SNLI.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 reports percent change from BART-large, DEBERTA-large, and Flan-T5-large baselines across accuracy/precision/recall/F1; e.g., on TOXIGEN, DEBERTA original accuracy 82.77 with kNN +0.96, DT -0.22, L-means -0.53; the worst losses are DT recall (-11.87 on DEBERTA TOXIGEN); on E-SNLI, DEBERTA original accuracy 91.75 with kNN -0.77 and BART L-means -2.82. Two-proportion z-tests at alpha = 0.05 flag 12.5% and 27% of cells.

key_findings.claim: Explanation design is framed as an explicit three-way tradeoff (performance, faithfulness, simplicity): showing all n consulted examples is fully faithful but can overload users, showing m < n is simpler but sacrifices fidelity by conscious decision, and shrinking n itself preserves fidelity at possible performance cost.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.1 and Table 2 define Cases I-III over which examples are used for inference versus explanation; per-model downsampling rules are specified (kNN: nearest m whose majority label matches; DT and L-means: most central leaf/cluster members whose majority label matches the prediction).

key_findings.claim: For removal-based contestation, greedy search over the wrapper box's own candidate example sets achieves 100% coverage and 100% correctness for kNN and L-means on both datasets, versus 27.45% coverage/about 27% correctness (TOXIGEN) and 89.83% coverage but at most 0.39% correctness (E-SNLI) for the influence-function baselines.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 with DEBERTA representations: kNN greedy finds verified flip sets with median size 211 (TOXIGEN) and 77.5 (E-SNLI); L-means also reaches 100/100 but with medians 6,377 and 140,523; DT covers only 12.02% and 3.23% because candidates are limited to leaf examples; Yang Fast/Slow (logistic regression + influence approximations) propose sets that almost never flip E-SNLI decisions, which the authors attribute to their binary-classification threshold formulation not carrying over to multi-class softmax.

key_findings.claim: The kNN flip-set search needs no retraining at all, making it orders of magnitude faster than every alternative.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 2 precomputes ranked neighbor lists and recomputes the unweighted majority vote over a sliding k-window after each removal; qualitative runtimes on a 48-core Xeon node: kNN under 1 second per example versus Yang Fast 3 minutes, Yang Slow 15 minutes, DT 5 minutes, and L-means 25 minutes per example on E-SNLI.

key_findings.claim: With zero-shot LLM representations, wrapper boxes strongly outperform zero-shot prompting on both tasks, but only after a supervised logistic-regression logit transformation of the embeddings.
key_findings.evidence: Tables 12-13: TOXIGEN accuracy rises from 61.17 (Llama2-7B zero-shot) to 82.23 (L-means) and from 55.64 (Gemma-7B) to 79.47; E-SNLI rises from 47.96 (Llama2-7B) to 73.03 (DT) and from 70.99 (Mistral-7B) to 81.94 (DT). Appendix H states mean-pooled penultimate embeddings are first mapped to logistic-regression logits because fitting wrapper boxes directly on raw embeddings 'can lead to severe performance degradation, particularly for L-means'.

anchors.section: Appendix H.1, evaluation setup and logit transformation

key_findings.claim: The training-data attribution is not counterfactually complete: the neural representations are fine-tuned on the full training set, so a removed subset S_t still influences predictions through the frozen features.
key_findings.evidence: Section 8.3 concedes that both this work and Yang et al. apply classifiers 'atop fixed feature representations, without considering counterfactual data conditions that would change feature representations'; in this work 'neural representations are fine-tuned on all training data and counterfactual training data conditions only impact wrapper box inference'. The recourse story therefore covers the wrapper vote but not the encoder, which is the component actually trained on the contested data.

key_findings.claim: The perfect coverage/correctness of kNN and L-means is close to guaranteed by construction, so the informative comparison metrics are subset size and runtime, on which the results are mixed.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 1 removes prediction-labeled candidates and directly verifies flips by refitting the lightweight wrapper (or recomputing the vote), iterating until no reduction is possible; for a majority-vote model, exhausting same-labeled candidates must eventually flip the vote, unlike the Yang baselines, which only propose sets whose estimated effect crosses a threshold without verification. Median flip sets of 211 (kNN TOXIGEN), 6,377, and 140,523 (L-means) examples are far above what a user could inspect, a burden the authors themselves flag via the information-overload discussion and the robustness reading of large S_t.

key_findings.claim: The LLM ablation conflates the wrapper-box contribution with supervised probing, weakening both the zero-shot framing and the interpretability claim for that setting.
key_findings.evidence: The comparison is zero-shot prompting versus classifiers trained on labeled training data over LLM embeddings, so most of the reported gap plausibly comes from supervision itself; because the wrapper features are logistic-regression logits (a 1-to-3 dimensional learned projection), 'similar training examples' are defined in a space already shaped by a supervised linear model, and no plain logistic-regression baseline accuracy is reported for the LLM setting to isolate the case-based component.

key_findings.claim: The paper's own qualitative-explanation practice illustrates the fidelity risk it theorizes: single-nearest-example explanations shown to users are Case II (unfaithful) and sometimes carry a label disagreeing with the prediction.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix G notes that presenting only the closest training point 'does not constitute a faithful explanation', that row 3 of Table 10 shows the prediction disagreeing with the closest example's label, and cites Lakkaraju and Bastani on misleading users when unfaithful explanations are believed faithful; the paper still argues such explanations are useful intuition.

key_findings.claim: Statistical and experimental hygiene is thin for the headline comparability claim: single run with seed 42, no hyperparameter search, and an unpaired two-proportion z-test on predictions from the same test set.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A states all results are single-run with seed 42, kNN uses k=5 chosen informally from a narrow range, DT depth 3 'was not tuned', and E-SNLI swaps in LightGBM because scikit-learn 'does not scale well'; Appendix B computes z-scores treating baseline and treatment accuracies as independent binomials, although both models classify the identical test instances, where a paired test (e.g., McNemar) would be standard; Appendix B.3 argues small significant differences are operationally invisible, citing Sparck Jones's 5%/10% rule of thumb.

method.core_idea: Keep the neural model as a task-specific encoder only: fine-tune it as usual, extract penultimate-layer representations, and let transparent case-based classifiers (kNN, decision tree, labeled k-means) make the actual predictions, so that every decision is by construction determined by an identifiable set of training examples that can be shown, audited, or removed.
method.mechanism: After fine-tuning (BART-large, DEBERTA-large, Flan-T5-large) or zero-shot extraction (Llama2/3, Mistral, Gemma instruct models), per-token penultimate hidden states are mean-pooled into sentence vectors and stored in memory. kNN (unweighted, k=5, K-D tree retrieval, Euclidean distance) predicts by majority vote of neighbors; the decision tree (depth 3, or LightGBM for E-SNLI, minimum 20 samples per leaf) predicts by majority vote over the reached leaf's training examples; L-means assigns each input the majority label of the nearest cluster centroid. For contestation, Algorithm 1 ranks the model's own candidate examples (neighbors, leaf members, or cluster members), filters those sharing the predicted label, removes them in B=10 bins with verification by refitting the wrapper, then refines iteratively below a 100-example threshold; kNN admits a retraining-free variant that re-evaluates the majority vote over the ranked neighbor list. In the LLM setting, embeddings are first projected to logistic-regression logits before wrapper fitting.
assumptions: The fine-tuned encoder's penultimate space is linearly well-separated enough that classic classifiers match the neural head's accuracy.

Euclidean proximity in the learned representation space identifies training examples that users will recognize as relevant analogies (Appendix D concedes human-model similarity alignment is unverified).
Faithfulness to the wrapper box's inference procedure is the right target, even though the wrapper is a substitute for, not an explanation of, the neural model.

Removing training examples from the wrapper's candidate set while freezing the encoder representations constitutes meaningful counterfactual attribution, despite the encoder having been trained on the removed examples.
Majority-vote flip verification by cheap wrapper refits is an acceptable stand-in for full-pipeline retraining.
Training data is available and showable at inference time (explanations are impossible for private corpora).
For LLM representations, a supervised logistic-logit projection preserves the case-based interpretability story while fixing raw-embedding performance collapse.

techniques.role: Mean-pools per-token hidden states from the layer before the classification/generation head into sentence vectors that serve as the feature space for all wrapper models.
Predicts by unweighted vote of the k=5 nearest training examples, making the consulted neighbors the complete faithful explanation.
Learns shallow hyperplane rules and predicts by majority vote over the reached leaf's training members, trading example diversity for rule-based structure.
L-means reduces the training set to L cluster centroids labeled by member majority vote; inference is nearest-centroid, explained via the centroid-inducing examples.
When showing m < n examples, selects the nearest/most-central examples whose majority label matches the prediction to keep simplified explanations consistent.
Derives flip sets S_t by chunked removal (B=10 bins) of prediction-labeled candidates with verified refits, then iterative refinement below a 100-example threshold.
Exploits vote recomputation over precomputed ranked neighbor lists to verify prediction flips in under a second per example without any model refit.
Maps zero-shot LLM embeddings through fitted logistic-regression logits before wrapper fitting; empirically necessary to avoid severe degradation, especially for L-means.
Flags wrapper-vs-baseline metric differences at alpha = 0.05 by treating correct/incorrect prediction counts as independent binomials.

evaluations.setting: TOXIGEN binary toxicity (9,900 human-labeled GPT-3-generated statements, 3:1 benign:toxic, stratified 70/20/10 split) with fine-tuned BART-large, DEBERTA-large, Flan-T5-large
evaluations.metric: Percent change in macro accuracy/precision/recall/F1 vs each transformer, with two-proportion z-tests
evaluations.result: 6 of 48 comparisons significant, 3 favoring the wrapper box; e.g., DEBERTA kNN +0.96 accuracy/+5.02 precision/-5.63 recall; the largest degradation is DT recall -11.87 on DEBERTA.
evaluations.baseline: Each fine-tuned transformer's own linear-head predictions (DEBERTA best at 82.77 accuracy)

evaluations.setting: E-SNLI three-way NLI (569,033 pairs, predefined splits, balanced labels), same three transformers; DT implemented as LightGBM for scale
evaluations.metric: Percent change in accuracy/precision/recall/F1 with the same z-test procedure
evaluations.result: 13 of 48 comparisons significant; changes are small in magnitude (largest L-means on BART, about -2.8 accuracy); L-means clusters are noisier than TOXIGEN's near-clean two clusters.
evaluations.baseline: Fine-tuned transformers (DEBERTA 91.75 accuracy); Appendix F cluster purity contextualizes the L-means drop

evaluations.setting: Removal-based decision flipping on both datasets using DEBERTA representations, versus Yang et al. (2023) Fast/Slow influence-function selectors on logistic regression
evaluations.metric: Coverage (% of test inputs with a proposed S_t), correctness (% whose removal verifiably flips the prediction), median |S_t| among verified flips
evaluations.result: kNN greedy: 100/100 coverage/correctness with medians 211 (TOXIGEN) and 77.5 (E-SNLI); L-means: 100/100 with medians 6,377 and 140,523; DT greedy: 12.02 and 3.23 coverage; Yang Fast/Slow: 27.45 coverage/about 27 correctness on TOXIGEN and 89.83 coverage but 0.39/0.11 correctness on E-SNLI.
evaluations.baseline: Yang Fast (influence-estimated output change over threshold tau) and Yang Slow (iterative parameter-change approximation), both limited to convex linear classifiers

evaluations.setting: Reproduction of Yang et al. (2023) on their five original datasets (movie reviews, essays, emotion, hate speech, tweet sentiment) with BERT [cls] features and logistic regression
evaluations.result: Reproduced numbers are comparable to the originals (e.g., movie reviews 64.22 coverage vs reported values), validating the baseline implementation; low essays coverage (7.47) mirrors the original 11-12%.
evaluations.baseline: Yang et al.'s published Table 2 results, with acknowledged split/seed and L2-penalty differences

evaluations.setting: Zero-shot LLM representations (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-7B, all instruct) with logit-projected embeddings; E-SNLI training subsampled to 10,000
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, F1, precision, recall vs zero-shot prompting of the same LLM
evaluations.result: Wrapper boxes beat prompting everywhere: TOXIGEN best case 55.64 to 79.47 accuracy (Gemma, L-means); E-SNLI best case 47.96 to 73.03 (Llama2, DT); DT is consistently strongest on E-SNLI (Mistral 81.94 vs 70.99 zero-shot).
evaluations.baseline: Zero-shot classification prompts (Table 14); no fine-tuned or in-context-learning LLM baseline, and no LR-only accuracy reported

limitations: Author-stated (p.9, 8.1): wrapper boxes must store training data (or cached representative subsets) to furnish example-based explanations, and classic-model compute/storage costs carry over; some wrappers may be slower than the neural head.
Author-stated (p.10, 8.2): only the contestation use case is evaluated; claimed end-user benefits (simulatability, trust, data debugging) are untested, with user studies deferred to future work.

Author-stated (p.10, 8.3): removal counterfactuals ignore conditions that would change the learned representations; the encoder is fine-tuned on all training data, so removed examples still act through frozen features. Model- and training-regime counterfactuals are also out of scope.
Author-stated (p.10, 8.3 and p.18, C.4): found subsets are guaranteed neither minimal nor unique, and large S_t sets complicate auditing even though they can signal robustness.
Author-stated (p.20, Appendix D): Euclidean similarity in the learned space may diverge from human similarity judgments, and explanations are impossible when training data is private.
Author-stated (p.24, H.1): LLM experiments are zero-shot only, use a 10,000-example E-SNLI subsample, and raw mean-pooled embeddings required a supervised logistic-logit projection to work.

Reviewer-identified: significance testing treats the two models' predictions on the same test set as independent binomial samples; a paired test would likely change which of the 48-cell differences are significant, and all results are single-run (seed 42) without variance estimates.

Reviewer-identified: 'largely comparable' aggregates over cells that include double-digit recall drops (DT -11.87 recall on TOXIGEN DEBERTA), and the comparability argument partially leans on a noticeability heuristic (Sparck Jones 5% rule) rather than equivalence testing.

Reviewer-identified: the Yang comparison is asymmetric by design — the baselines estimate removal effects without verification while the greedy method verifies flips by refitting — so coverage/correctness superiority partly reflects the evaluation protocol rather than better attribution quality; subset-size and runtime are the more informative axes.

Reviewer-identified: evaluation covers two English classification tasks with one representation model (DEBERTA) for the attribution study; generation tasks, multi-label settings, and non-English data are untouched.
failure_modes: When clusters are homogeneous, L-means flip sets balloon (median 140,523 on E-SNLI), making removal-based recourse computationally verifiable but practically meaningless for a contesting user.
DT contestation collapses (3-12% coverage) whenever the reached leaf contains too few opposing-label candidates, since its search space is only the leaf's members.
Simplified m < n explanations can display an example whose label contradicts the prediction (Table 10 row 3), which may mislead users who assume fidelity.
If penultimate representations are not cleanly separable (noisier E-SNLI clusters), centroid-based wrappers lose accuracy relative to the neural head.
Raw zero-shot LLM embeddings without the supervised logit projection degrade wrapper performance severely, so the pipeline silently depends on labeled data even in the 'zero-shot' regime.

For skewed label distributions, threshold-based influence baselines break down (Yang et al. on TOXIGEN/E-SNLI), but the wrapper approach inherits its own skew sensitivity through untuned tree depth and k.
Attribution assertions can be invalidated end-to-end: retraining the encoder without S_t could restore the original prediction, since the representation still encodes the removed examples.
reusable_insights: A fine-tuned network's penultimate space is often linearly separable enough that simple case-based classifiers match the head's accuracy, so interpretability can be added post hoc by swapping the decision layer instead of retraining the architecture.

Scoping faithfulness to a substitute model that actually makes the deployed prediction (rather than explaining the original model post hoc) converts the faithfulness problem into a design property, at the cost of changing what is deployed.
The performance/faithfulness/simplicity triad with explicit m-of-n accounting (Cases I-III) is a portable framework for any example-based explanation system.

Verified greedy removal over a model's own candidate example sets gives exact, deterministic flip sets whenever the model is cheap to refit, and majority-vote models admit retraining-free verification via vote recomputation on ranked candidate lists.

Coverage/correctness of removal-based recourse should always be read jointly with subset size and runtime, since vote-based models can trivially achieve perfect coverage with uninformatively large sets.
Supervised low-dimensional projections (e.g., LR logits) can rescue classic models on raw LLM embeddings, but they re-introduce a learned component that any interpretability claim must account for.
open_questions: Do end users actually contest, trust, or debug better with wrapper-box explanations than with post-hoc attributions? No user study exists yet.
How much of the attribution survives end-to-end counterfactual retraining, i.e., re-fine-tuning the encoder without S_t — does the prediction still flip?
Can minimal or approximately minimal flip sets be found with guarantees, and how do bin count B and threshold phi trade off subset size against compute?
How would wrapper boxes compare against stronger LLM baselines (few-shot ICL, fine-tuning) and against a bare logistic-regression probe in the LLM setting?
Does the approach extend beyond sentence-level classification to generation, retrieval, or multi-label tasks where 'the consulted training examples' is harder to define?
Can representation spaces be aligned to human similarity judgments (per Appendix D) without sacrificing the accuracy that makes the wrapper swap viable?
How sensitive are the comparability results to k, tree depth, cluster count L, and random seed, none of which were tuned or varied?

competitive_landscape.title: Deep k-Nearest Neighbors: Towards Confident, Interpretable and Robust Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct conceptual predecessor the paper explicitly generalizes
competitive_landscape.difference: DkNN runs kNN over every layer's representations to produce conformal credibility/confidence estimates aimed largely at adversarial robustness; wrapper boxes use only the penultimate layer, broaden the wrapper family to decision trees and labeled clustering, quantify the m-of-n faithfulness/simplicity tradeoff, and add the removal-based contestation evaluation that DkNN lacks.

competitive_landscape.title: How Many and Which Training Points Would Need to be Removed to Flip this Prediction?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct baseline for the contestation task and source of its formulation
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. approximate minimal removal sets with influence functions for convex, twice-differentiable classifiers (logistic regression) and propose sets without verifying flips; the wrapper-box greedy search verifies every flip by refitting lightweight case-based models (or vote recomputation for kNN), covers non-convex wrappers, and empirically dominates on coverage/correctness while producing larger subsets in some settings.

competitive_landscape.title: ProtoTEx: Explaining Model Decisions with Prototype Tensors
competitive_landscape.relationship: Inherently interpretable competitor from the same research group
competitive_landscape.difference: ProtoTEx trains the full network with latent prototype tensors interleaved into the architecture and explains via examples nearest to influential prototypes, requiring end-to-end training and yielding at best partially faithful example attribution; wrapper boxes require no neural retraining, attribute to the actual voting training examples, and are architecture-agnostic.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational post-hoc training-data attribution method the paper contrasts against
competitive_landscape.difference: Influence functions estimate each training point's effect via inverse-Hessian approximations at O(np^2 + p^3) cost and remain post-hoc estimates that can be fragile for deep non-convex models; wrapper boxes make attribution exact and deterministic for the substitute case-based classifier at the price of explaining a different model than the neural network.

competitive_landscape.title: Explaining and Improving Model Behavior with k Nearest Neighbor Representations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior kNN-over-representations work for NLP interpretation
competitive_landscape.difference: Rajani et al. use kNN over fine-tuned representations chiefly as a diagnostic — to reveal artifacts, calibrate confidence, and improve robustness of the original model whose predictions remain neural; wrapper boxes instead promote the case-based model to the deployed predictor so that the retrieved examples are the decision procedure, and extend the recipe to trees and clustering plus recourse evaluation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a general, model/task/dataset-agnostic 'wrapper box' pipeline that preserves neural predictive performance while providing fully faithful, example-based attribution by design, with no neural retraining and no expensive influence computation, plus higher coverage and correctness than prior work at identifying removal sets that flip decisions, generalizing that task beyond linear models.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Table 1 positions the work against prototypes, concept layers, influence functions, and DkNN on training cost, runtime, and fidelity; experiments span seven language models, two datasets, three wrapper models, and four metrics, with the contestation comparison against Yang et al. (2023) and a five-dataset reproduction of that baseline.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The individual ingredients are old — kNN/decision trees on neural activations date to Caruana et al. (1999), and DkNN (2018) and Rajani et al. (2020) already ran kNN over transformer representations. What is new is the combination: elevating several classic models to the deployed predictor with an explicit m-of-n faithfulness/simplicity accounting, and especially the verified greedy flip-set search with a retraining-free kNN variant, which is the paper's strongest empirical differentiator over influence-function selectors. The headline 'faithful attribution' is narrower than it sounds: it holds for the wrapper substitute, not the neural model or the encoder trained on the contested data (acknowledged in 8.3), and the coverage/correctness dominance is partly built into the verify-by-refit protocol. Novelty is therefore best characterized as a useful synthesis plus a new, more rigorous evaluation of removal-based recourse, rather than a new attribution mechanism.
